subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Event Horizon Telescope
description: A 60-second lesson on The Event Horizon Telescope.

hook.text: In 2019, scientists combined radio dishes worldwide into one Earth-sized virtual telescope—and photographed a black hole.

buildup.text: The Event Horizon Telescope linked observatories from Hawaii to Antarctica using atomic clocks for perfect timing.

discovery.text: The target was M87*—a 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole 55 million light-years away. The image showed a glowing ring.

twist.text: The ring isn't the black hole—it's superheated gas orbiting just outside the event horizon. The dark center is the shadow.

climax.text: In 2022, EHT imaged Sgr A*, our own galaxy's black hole. Two shadows captured—one far away, one right at home.

punchline.text: An Earth-sized telescope. Two black hole shadows. History in pixels.

quiz.question: What does the dark center of the EHT black hole image represent?
options: The shadow of the black hole where light cannot escape
The surface of the black hole itself
A gap in the accretion disk caused by the jet

details.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a global network of radio telescopes synchronized to act as a single Earth-sized dish using very-long-baseline interferometry. This virtual telescope achieved the angular resolution needed to image black hole shadows, producing the historic M87 and Sgr A* images.
details.whyItMatters: The EHT demonstrated that international collaboration and clever engineering can overcome seemingly impossible observational challenges. It proved that black hole shadows could be imaged, opening a new era of horizon-scale astrophysics.
takeaways: Global network of radio telescopes acting as one giant dish
Uses very-long-baseline interferometry for extreme resolution
Produced the first images of black hole shadows

faq.question: How does the EHT achieve such high resolution?
faq.answer: Resolution depends on telescope diameter and observing wavelength. By linking telescopes across the globe, the EHT effectively becomes an Earth-diameter dish at 1.3mm wavelength. This achieves angular resolution of about 20 microarcseconds — equivalent to reading a newspaper in New York from Paris.

faq.question: How much data does the EHT produce?
faq.answer: Each observing campaign generates roughly 5 petabytes of data recorded on hard drives at each telescope site. The data is physically shipped to computing centers because it exceeds internet bandwidth. Correlation and image reconstruction then takes months of computation.
